text: A is attack, built for hitting targets on land or at sea. B is bomber. C is cargo. F is fighter.
The Air Force even gave the F to the F one seventeen Nighthawk, a stealth jet built for ground attack, with no official air-to-air role.
For years, people were convinced a secret F nineteen stealth fighter existed. In July nineteen eighty-six, the Air Force sealed off a crash site in California, and the rumors exploded.
The rest of the list works the same way. W is weather reconnaissance, which is why the Air Force's hurricane hunters are W C one thirties.
And M and U look alike, but they're split by the kind of mission. M aircraft fly combat and special operations. U aircraft fly support, like the U H sixty Black Hawk.
The F forty-seven was chosen partly to honor the P forty-seven Thunderbolt, and nineteen forty-seven, the year the Air Force was founded.
Missiles get the same treatment, with three letters of their own.
The first letter says where it's launched from. A is air. R is a surface ship. U is underwater. L is a silo. And B means more than one kind of launcher.
The second letter is the job. I means intercepting targets in the air. G means attacking targets on land or at sea.
And the third says what it is. M for guided missile. R for a rocket that can't be steered once it's launched.
So an A I M nine reads as air-launched, intercept, guided missile.
The Sparrow shows how flexible this is. Fired from a jet, it's the A I M seven. Fired from a ship, it becomes the R I M seven Sea Sparrow. Same number, new first letter.
And an R G M eighty-four D Harpoon reads the same way. Ship-launched. Surface attack. Guided missile. Design eighty-four. Fourth modification.
Now, a longer aircraft name: the H H sixty G.

The first H is the modified mission: search and rescue. The second H is the vehicle type: helicopter. Sixty is the design number, the same family as the U H sixty Black Hawk. And G is the series letter.
In fact, some of them started life as Black Hawks that were modified for rescue, and the mission letter followed the new job.
